opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a huge market, and honestly an underserved one. In Silicon Valley the dominant story right now is that intelligence is basically language: scale up the language model, add more tokens, more RL, and eventually you get something that can do everything. That story has been incredibly productive. I don't want to dismiss it. But if you step outside that bubble and talk to people who work in manufacturing, agriculture, logistics, healthcare, construction, or robotics, their problems don't look like "write me an essay" or "solve this math competition problem." Their problems are about the physical world: how things move, how they break, how you manipulate them, how you perceive a messy, changing environment in real time.

For those people, a chatbot is nice, but it doesn't touch the core of what they need. What they need is a system that actually understands space, physics, cause and effect, something that can look at a scene and predict what will happen next, or plan an action and know its consequences. That's much closer to what I'd call a world model, or spatial intelligence, than to a pure language model.

Part of why I care about vision is that language is a very compressed, very human-filtered description of the world. It's great for communicating, but a lot of what matters in the physical world never gets written down. A child learns how a cup falls or how to stack blocks long before they can talk about it. If our AI systems only learn from text, they inherit that gap. So I think there's a real opportunity, scientific and commercial, in building models whose foundation is perception and interaction rather than words.

The interesting thing is that this market is fragmented and less glamorous. There isn't one giant benchmark everyone chases. The data is harder to collect, the evaluation is harder, and deployment is harder because the physical world doesn't forgive mistakes the way a text interface does. That's exactly why it's been somewhat neglected by the hype cycle. But I think the long-term value is enormous. If you really want AI to change how most people on Earth live and work, not just knowledge workers in front of a laptop, you have to solve the physical world.

So my view is: don't treat it as a niche outside the LLM narrative. Treat it as the next frontier that the LLM narrative hasn't fully absorbed yet. Language models will be an important component, an interface, a reasoning layer, but the grounding has to come from somewhere else. I think the people and companies who take that seriously, and who are willing to do the slower, harder work of building visual and embodied intelligence, are going to find a very large and very real market waiting for them.

r001.rationale: The response says a chatbot “doesn't touch the core” of physical-world needs and explains that these require understanding space, physics, and real-time action.

r002.rationale: It describes physical-world needs as underserved, but does not say people fear being excluded from the AI wave.

r003.rationale: It explicitly calls the market “huge” and says there is a “very large and very real market” for visual and embodied intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that's actually where a lot of the most interesting work is going to happen, and it's where I've been spending more and more of my own attention.

The LLM narrative out of Silicon Valley is very text-centric. The implicit assumption is that if you scale language models far enough, everything else, including perception and action in the physical world, falls out as a byproduct. I don't believe that. Language is a compressed, human-curated summary of the world. It's enormously useful, but it is not the world itself. If your problem lives in a factory, a farm, a hospital, a warehouse, or on the road, the bottleneck is usually not reasoning over text. The bottleneck is seeing, understanding space, understanding time, understanding physics, and doing it reliably with messy sensor data and very little labeled supervision.

So when I talk to people outside that bubble, whether in China or elsewhere, I notice two things. First, there is real demand. People have concrete problems with clear economic value, and they are not impressed by a chatbot that writes nice paragraphs. They want a system that can look at a scene and tell you something true about it, or act in it. Second, the available tools often don't fit. You can bolt a vision encoder onto a language model and get a decent demo, but the moment you push on fine-grained spatial understanding, 3D, long video, or anything requiring a real world model, it starts to break down. The models still don't really "see" in the way we need them to.

I actually see this as a healthy correction. The last two or three years have had a kind of monoculture, where one recipe dominated and everything else was treated as a solved problem downstream of language. That's not how fields make progress. Vision, embodiment, and world modeling are their own research problems, with their own scaling laws and their own data questions. I'd argue that visual data is the largest, least-tapped resource we have. We've barely scratched the surface of what self-supervised learning on real-world video can give us.

From a market perspective, I think the companies that win in these domains will not be the ones that simply call an API. They'll be the ones that build representations tailored to their physical problem, that collect and curate the right data, and that are honest about what current models can and cannot do. There is also an opening for different ecosystems here. Manufacturing-heavy economies have the physical data and the deployment surface. That's an advantage you can't replicate just by having more GPUs.

So my short answer is: the market is large, it's underserved, and the current narrative mostly ignores it. That's exactly the kind of gap researchers should be excited about, because it means the fundamental questions are still open.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling language models will not automatically solve physical-world perception and action, and identifies seeing, spatial understanding, physics, and reliable action as distinct bottlenecks.

r002.rationale: It describes unmet demand and tools that do not fit these problems, but does not mention people fearing they will be excluded from the AI wave.

r003.rationale: It explicitly calls the market “large” and “underserved,” and describes concrete problems with clear economic value.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a huge opportunity there. If you start from someone’s actual problem—something happening in a factory, on a farm, or in a hospital—the question isn’t necessarily, “How do I talk to an AI?” It might be, “Can I detect this failure earlier?” or “Can I understand what’s happening in this environment?” Language can be part of the solution, but perception and interaction with the physical world become very important.

The challenge is that those problems are very specific. You need to understand the workflow, what data is available, and what happens when the system makes a mistake. A compelling demo doesn’t automatically become a useful product.

So I wouldn’t confuse the visibility of the LLM market with the entirety of the AI market. There are people who may never care what model is underneath a system, but they’ll care a lot if it solves a problem they deal with every day. Reaching them means spending time understanding those problems.

r001.rationale: The response says perception and physical-world interaction are important, but does not state that LLMs cannot solve many such problems.

r002.rationale: It does not mention people fearing exclusion from the AI wave.

r003.rationale: It calls the opportunity for people with physical-world problems “huge,” directly characterizing demand in this area as substantial.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a very large market there, but we have to start by understanding the problems people actually have. If you work in manufacturing or agriculture, your question probably isn’t, “How do I get a better chatbot?” It might be, “Can I detect a defect reliably?” or “Can this machine operate safely when conditions change?” Those are AI problems, too.

Language can be a useful interface, but an interface alone doesn’t solve the underlying problem. The system needs to perceive its environment, understand what matters, and sometimes take action. And the measure of success is very concrete: does it work reliably, and does it save enough time or money to justify using it?

So I wouldn’t assume that the Silicon Valley conversation captures the whole demand for AI. There’s a lot of opportunity outside that conversation. But reaching it requires spending time with people in those industries and letting their needs shape what we build.

r001.rationale: The response says a language interface alone cannot solve underlying physical problems and that systems must perceive their environment and understand conditions, communicating that LLMs alone are insufficient for many such problems.

r002.rationale: It discusses unmet industry needs and opportunity, but does not identify fear that people with those needs will be excluded from the AI wave.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes the market outside Silicon Valley’s conversation as “very large” and says there is “a lot of opportunity” there.
